newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's Chirac breaks uneasy peace with left.
newsitem.headline: France's Chirac breaks uneasy peace with left.

text.p: Conservative President Jacques Chirac has broken an uneasy peace with France's new leftist government, firing a volley of criticism at Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin just six weeks after he came to power.

Chirac, in a traditional broadcast appearance on France's July 14 national day, criticised the left on policies ranging from privatisation to nuclear power, Europe and immigration, prompting leftist leaders to charge on Tuesday that Chirac was acting like an opposition leader rather than head of state.
"I think Jacques Chirac went too far in his criticisms," said Socialist Party leader Francois Hollande, reminding him that the previous rightist government had just been voted out of power.
"The government sets policy while the president is the guardian of our institutions. And I think we should continue to maintain this balance," Hollande told Radio Monte Carlo.

Chirac, in his first television interview since being shorn of much of his power by a left-wing victory in parliamentary elections six weeks ago, asserted a broad role for himself that went well beyond the traditional presidential domains of defence and foreign affairs.

He said the constitution gave him "a pre-eminent role, the last word" on matters ranging from the transition to a single European currency and maintaining social cohesion to upholding France's high-technology industries.
He also scotched brewing leftist plans to trim his term to five years from seven.

Though Chirac had previously endorsed the idea, Jospin had out of courtesy for the president said he would seek a referendum on a shorter presidential term only if Chirac gave his approval ahead of time.

Hollande dismissed the president's criticisms as "just words" that had not damaged the delicate power-sharing relationship between the left and right but pointedly added that it was now up to Chirac to show a willingess to be constructive.
The president's criticisms laid out a roadmap of potential conflicts with the government, with the transition to the single European currency near the top of the list.
Chirac said the planned 1999 launch date and the agreed conditions for a single European currency must be respected.

"It would have very serious conquences for France not to do it -- very, very serious -- we would isolate ourselves," he said, adding that the government could achieve the Maastricht Treaty target of three percent if it held down spending.
Hollande dismissed the notion that it would be up to the president to assure the transition to the euro, insisting the decision would be up to the government and to parliament.
"There will be a discussion in parliament and in these conditions, no one can claim the title of privileged defender of the nation to make or not make the euro," Hollande said.
"I think we will have to base our decision on the interests of the country," he said.

Chirac's broad attack on Jospin's young government dominated the French media on Tuesday, signalling that his words had the desired effect of putting the public as well as the government on notice of his potential to make trouble for Jospin.
"Chirac Demolition Man," bannered the daily France-Soir.
"Was it necessary for Mr Chirac to assume so soon the position of battle leader for the opposition?" asked the left-leaning daily Le Monde.
"He said it with a smile but his meaning was clear: Jospin has either done nothing or he has done the opposite of what he should have done," said an editorial in the centre-left daily Liberation.
